explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "I bow my knees before the Father," and he's writing as a prisoner (Ephesians 3:14; 3:1). Whatever his chains were doing, his knees were still free to bow. I think a lot of us could learn from a man who prays from right where he is.

Nice thought, friend, but that's not what Paul says here. The text says, "I bow my knees before the Father" (Ephesians 3:14). Lifted hands show up in other places in Scripture, but in this verse Paul is down on his knees. I lift things with my mustache all day, but the knees are Paul's move this time.

I'd pay good money to hear that, baker, but it's not in this verse. Paul says, "I bow my knees before the Father" (Ephesians 3:14). No standing, no song, just a man on his knees. Sometimes the simple picture is the right one.

Right on, friend. Paul asks that "He may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). Notice he starts with strength, not a to-do list. I think a man in chains knows how much a person needs it.

I get why you'd pick it, baker, because trouble is the first thing most of us pray about. But Paul doesn't ask that here. He asks that the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). The ask is for strength on the inside.

Ha, I'd sign up for that one, friend. But it's not what Paul asks. He prays that the Father "may strengthen you with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). Strength for the inside, not a smoother road.

That's the one, baker. Paul says the strength comes "through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). The Spirit is the Holy Spirit, one of the three I believe in. The power comes through Him.

Close to home, friend, since Paul is an apostle himself. But he doesn't say the power comes through apostles. He says it's "through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). Paul is the one praying here, and he points to the Spirit.

Prophets matter in Scripture, baker, but they're not named here. Paul asks the Father to strengthen them "with power through His Spirit in your inner being" (Ephesians 3:16). The Spirit is the answer. No middleman needed.

explanations.answer: Christ may dwell in their hearts
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Paul prays for strength "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). Dwell means to settle in and stay. That's a lot better than a visit.

Whoa, friend, that's a tough crowd you're picturing. Paul doesn't mention enemies in this prayer. He asks for strength "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). The goal is Christ at home in their hearts.

explanations.answer: They may earn a great reward
explanations.explanation: I see the thinking, baker, but Paul isn't talking about earning anything here. He says the strength is "so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith" (Ephesians 3:17). It's about Christ living in them, through faith.

Not quite, friend. Paul says they will have power "together with all the saints" to comprehend it (Ephesians 3:18). So nobody is grasping it all alone. It's a group effort, and that's good news for those of us who can't hold much at once.

Yes, baker. Paul says they'll have power, "together with all the saints, to comprehend the length and width and height and depth" (Ephesians 3:18). It's a shared grasp. The saints do this one side by side.

That's right, baker. Paul says "the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). Four directions, and every one of them is love. I'd need a bigger cookie box to measure that.

Good word, friend, and the kingdom is a big theme in Scripture. But Paul isn't measuring it here. He says "the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). The word is love.

Wisdom is a fine thing, baker, but it's not the word in this verse. Paul says "the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ" (Ephesians 3:18-19). Love is what he wants them to comprehend.

explanations.answer: It's bigger than our minds can hold
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul calls it "this love that surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19). Surpasses means it goes beyond what we can wrap our heads around. And he still prays that we'd know it. Quite a thing.

explanations.answer: It's only for the very wise
explanations.explanation: Nope, friend, and I'm glad. Paul prays that they would "know this love that surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19), and he's praying it for the saints in Ephesus. Surpassing knowledge means it's bigger than our minds, not that it's kept for the smart ones. I once spent years in a drawer with a key that couldn't find its door, so I'm no genius either.

explanations.answer: It fades once you learn it
explanations.explanation: Other way around, baker. Paul says this love "surpasses knowledge" (Ephesians 3:19). It stays bigger than what we can learn, so there's always more. Nothing about it runs out.

That's the one, friend. Paul says God "is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). Immeasurably means you can't get out a ruler. Whatever you're picturing, He's able to go past it.
Ha, that's a modest God you're picturing, baker. Paul says He "is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). Immeasurably is a lot more than a little. Think bigger.
Nice try, friend, but Paul goes further. He says God "is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine" (Ephesians 3:20). Not just what we ask. Way past it.

explanations.answer: In the church and in Christ Jesus
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul writes, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). Two places, side by side. That's a whole lot of glory going to the right Person.

Good guess, friend, since the temple is a big deal in Scripture. But Paul doesn't mention it here. He says, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). The church and Christ Jesus are the places.

That sounds right, baker, and heaven is surely full of glory. But Paul doesn't say it here. He writes, "to Him be the glory in the church and in Christ Jesus" (Ephesians 3:21). Those are the two places he names.
Not quite, friend. Paul says the glory is "throughout all generations, forever and ever" (Ephesians 3:21). That's a lot more than his own generation. It keeps going.
You got it, baker. Paul says, "throughout all generations, forever and ever" (Ephesians 3:21). It's not just his own time. Every generation gets to join in, and that includes ours.
